title: Briatore: Mercedes in talks over buying Otro Capital’s stake in Alpine F1
content:
Mercedes is one of the multiple groups in talks over buying Otro Capital’s shares in Alpine’s Formula 1 team, Flavio Briatore revealed during Friday’s news conference at the Chinese Grand Prix weekend.

One of the other groups that’s shown interest involves former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner.

The confirmation of Mercedes’ interest comes after The Telegraph reported earlier this week that team boss Toto Wolff was leading the bid.

It’s been no secret that the American private equity firm has been looking to sell its stake in the Enstone-based team, but Mercedes’ involvement adds a unique twist given it supplies the engines and gearboxes to Alpine, until the end of 2030 with the current deal.

Briatore, de facto team boss of Alpine, made sure to clarify during the news conference that the negotiation is with Mercedes, not with Wolff (who has had shares in two other F1 teams before — Williams and Mercedes).

Briatore estimated that there’s “three or four potential buyers” and gave a strong “no” when asked if he was tempted to invest and buy the 24 percent stake, saying so multiple times.

“I’m just looking at what’s going on and just watching what’s going on. For us, we have no communication with Toto in this moment. So, if somebody buys the shares, we are very happy,” Briatore added.

Earlier this week, a Mercedes spokesperson said: “Mercedes is a key strategic partner of Alpine and we are being kept apprised of the latest developments.”

The 24 percent stake in the F1 team was bought by a consortium of three American firms in 2023: Maximum Effort Investments (Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney, who also own football club Wrexham), RedBird Capital Partners (the controlling owner of Italian club AC Milan) and Otro Capital, which features sports stars across different leagues – including Kansas City Chiefs players Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce, boxer Anthony Joshua and golfer Rory McIlroy.

The other 76 percent is owned by Renault Group. When asked in the press conference whether Briatore could guarantee Mercedes would not have an influence on Alpine’s operations or how it voted on the F1 Commission if Mercedes did purchase the stake, Alpine’s executive advisory said, “Normally, one company, the 75 percent, decide and the 25 percent is a passenger, and this is the reality.”

If Mercedes does purchase the partial ownership of Alpine, this wouldn’t be the first time that one entity owns a stake in two F1 teams. Red Bull has done so since 2006, when Racing Bulls (then-known as Toro Rosso) joined the grid, a year after Red Bull Racing made its debut. The junior team has gone through rebranding over the years, but the two sides have always had close ties. It’s an issue that McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown has previously raised.

“The thing I would like to see us as a sport focus on, and needs to sit on the regulations side, is the A/B team co-ownership I believe is a serious issue for the fairness of the sport for the fans,” he said during McLaren’s 2024 season launch. “That’s why it’s pretty much not allowed in any other form of major sport, and I’d like to see us as an industry focus on that before it gets to a level of being where Formula One once was, which was very out of balance because people are playing by the rules but a different set of rules.”

Audi’s Jonathan Wheatley didn’t see any concerns or conflicts of interest, when asked Friday if the team principal would have a concern over multi-team ownership, and he pointed out that “the sport has very, very clear governance.” And he is right. This isn’t banned, but there are strict rules, such as on the technical side to ensure fairness.
